body:
A FLAKE, FIXED NOW RATHER THAN MANAGED (CLAUDE.md's standing rule). `test/browser/*.test.ts` has
failed on `windows-latest` five times, always in TEARDOWN and never in an assertion. The most recent
is PR #375, job 93858433410:

    Error: EPERM, Permission denied: \\?\C:\Users\RUNNER~1\AppData\Local\Temp\loam-door-smoke-U7afGQ
      at Browser.close test/browser/cdp.ts:223:5
      at test/browser/funnel.test.ts:120:3
    Serialized Error: { errno: 1, code: 'EPERM', path: '...loam-door-smoke-U7afGQ', syscall: 'rm' }
    Test Files  1 failed | 197 passed (198)   Tests  1911 passed | 11 skipped

The same shape appeared on #362 and #368 and once before them, and then a FIFTH time on this
ticket's own PR #379 — a branch that adds one JSON file and no code (job 93863384075,
`loam-door-smoke-PjaG08`, `Test Files 1 failed | 198 passed`). Ubuntu is green on the same commits.
Attribution is not in doubt: on #375 the same branch ran Windows twice, run 31514604409 passed and
31514647623 failed, and the only difference between the two commits was one markdown link.

THE EVIDENCE THAT NAMES THE CAUSE. The `path` in the error is the profile ROOT, not a file inside
it, and the syscall is `rm`. Node had already removed the contents and failed on the directory
itself. Windows refuses to remove a directory while any handle beneath it is open, so something was
still holding the profile after Chrome's browser process was gone.

That something is Chrome's OTHER processes. `child.kill()` reaches the browser process alone; the
renderer, GPU and `crashpad_handler` processes are separate processes with their own handles under
`--user-data-dir`, and they outlive their parent by a short unbounded moment. `crashpad_handler` in
particular is deliberately outside the browser's job object.

WHAT WAS TRIED AND WAS NOT ENOUGH. PR #353 made `Browser.close()` await the child's real `exit` with
a 5s ceiling and gave `rmSync` `maxRetries: 10, retryDelay: 200`. Both are correct and both address
the PARENT. Neither reaches a child that is still alive, so the retries expire against a handle that
is still open.

THE FIX, in two halves.

  - Kill the TREE, not the process. On win32, `taskkill /T /F /PID <pid>` through `spawnSync` — no
    shell, argv as an array. It runs BEFORE the parent is awaited, because a tree walk needs a live
    parent: `taskkill` refuses a pid that has already exited, and the orphans it would have
    collected would outlive the call. The exit-await and the retrying removal both stay.
  - Never fail a rail on a scratch directory. If the removal still loses the race on win32, print
    one honest line naming the leftover path and continue. The profile is throwaway scratch in the
    runner's temp directory; this rail's job is proving the doors work in a real browser, not
    proving Windows released a handle. Every other platform still throws, because there a failed
    removal is a real defect.

WHERE THE CODE GOES, and why it is not all in `cdp.ts`. `test/browser/cdp.ts` is a FROZEN rail of
T143 (archived), so this ticket ships as the two-PR authorization dance: a declaration in
`scripts/rail-renames.json` that lands first, then the exempted edit. The declaration is kept as
small as a reviewer can check by hand — three pairs — because the new logic and all of its reasoning
live in a NEW file, `test/browser/teardown.ts`. Teardown hygiene is not one of T143's assertions,
and hygiene that has now needed four attempts belongs where it can be tuned without an authorization
round. `cdp.ts` keeps every assertion and every launch argument it had.

NO NEW RAILS ARE DECLARED. There is no new behaviour to pin: the doors are already railed by the
four browser suites, and the only assertion this change could add is one about a Windows handle,
which no Linux runner can make. The proof is the Windows leg staying green. Stated plainly rather
than dressed up: a rail glob that matches nothing would print `all checks passed` and protect
nothing.

THE CONTROLLED EXPERIMENT, run without meaning to. Three PRs sat in the same runner pool inside one
fifteen-minute window on 2026-08-11: #379 (the ticket, one JSON file), #380 (the authorization, one
JSON file) and #382 (the fix). Ubuntu passed on all three. On `windows-latest`:

    #379  FAIL  EPERM  loam-door-smoke-2vTQSX   test/browser/human-doors.test.ts
    #380  FAIL  EPERM  loam-door-smoke-n2AELk   test/browser/door-smoke.test.ts (2 files failed)
    #382  PASS

Two diffs that touch no code went red, the diff that changes the teardown went green, same window,
same pool. That is as close to an A/B as CI gives.

WHAT AN INDEPENDENT REVIEW FOUND, and it was right five times. The reviewer read the diff without
this ticket and without the PR body. Every finding was a report that could be false: the `taskkill`
result was discarded (a missing binary, an access denial and a not-found pid all looked like
success); the already-exited parent was named in the comment and unhandled in the code; the win32
catch swallowed EVERY error rather than the three codes a held handle produces; `kill()` EMITS on a
process caught mid-termination, which with no listener leaves `afterAll`; and the function's own
first line claimed to stop everything Chrome spawned when on POSIX it is one SIGTERM. The sixth
finding was that nothing railed any of it.

SO THERE IS A RAIL AFTER ALL, on the ground a POSIX runner can reach: `test/browser/teardown.test.ts`
asserts that `killTree` stops the process it is handed, that `dropProfile` removes the directory it
is handed, and — the two-sided half — that a removal which cannot succeed still THROWS off Windows.
The last one fails the moment the swallow leaks onto every platform. The header names the two claims
no POSIX runner can make: that the tree kill collects Chrome's renderer, GPU and crashpad children,
and that the win32 branch swallows those three codes and no others. `adlc hollow-test` agrees and
says so plainly: 12 mutants, 1 killed, and every survivor inside the Windows-only branch or in a
retry constant.

A SIBLING LEAK, FOUND BY THE SAME REVIEW AND LEFT FOR ITS OWN TICKET. `Browser.launch()` throws on
two paths — Chrome exited before serving CDP, and Chrome never wrote `DevToolsActivePort` — and
neither runs any teardown. The second leaves a LIVE Chrome and its whole profile behind, which is a
larger leak than the one this ticket closes. It is pre-existing, it needs its own pairs in
`scripts/rail-renames.json`, and folding it in here would widen an authorization Myk is already
reading. File it rather than smuggle it.

HOW WE KNOW IT WORKED: the `windows-latest` leg passes on the fix PR, and stays passing. If the
EPERM returns after this, the next step is not another retry budget — it is capturing which process
holds the handle (`handle.exe` / Process Explorer on the runner) before changing anything else.
title: The browser rail's teardown loses a race with Chrome's children on Windows — four red CI legs from a scratch directory
